extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers interested in the logic and method of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging the evidential force, scope, and application of inductive generalizations (both universal and approximate), including when to treat them as empirical laws, how to measure their certainty, and how to combine or apply approximate generalizations to particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformities of co-existence are empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities which obtain in the co-existence of phenomena (properties of kinds) are to be ranked among empirical laws and are amenable to the same rules as unresolved uniformities known to depend on causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no general axiom analogous to the law of causation for co-existences; therefore such uniformities cannot be treated with the same certainty as causal laws and must be accepted only as empirical within observed limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ultimate properties from causal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether a property is an ultimate property of a Kind (intrinsic) or an effect depending on causes; this distinction determines how generalizations about that property should be treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a property is an effect of causes, widespread observation of it establishes a common cause and an empirical law; if it is a property of Kind, the generalization can only be overturned by the discovery of a new Kind, and in either case certainty is limited to observational bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inapplicability of elimination methods to co-existences
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of elimination (Bacon's methods of Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations) that works for succession/causation does not apply to inquiries into co-existence (properties of kinds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because there is no guarantee that a property of objects must have an invariable co-existent analogous to an invariable antecedent for events, elimination cannot reliably determine the 'form' of co-existent properties; many attempts at such analysis lead to no result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure certainty by improbability that an exception remained unobserved
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of certainty of a generalization based solely on past observation is another phrase for the improbability that an exception, if it existed, could have so far remained unobserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast statements like 'All crows are black' as 'it is improbable that a non-black crow could have existed without our knowing' and evaluate how credible potential exceptions would be (e.g., accidental individual variation vs undiscovered Kind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret possible exceptions as accidental causes or new Kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: If a counter-instance to a generalization exists, it must be either (1) an accidental/causal variation (the property is not of Kind) or (2) an instance of a new Kind previously overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a white crow among black ones suggests causation/accident; discovery of a population of white crows elsewhere suggests a distinct Kind. Determine which interpretation fits before revising the generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical generalizations limited to observed time, place, and circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations about co-existence, unless grounded in causation, ought not to be presumed true beyond the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which observations were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such generalizations must be ready to be given up on the occurrence of new anomalies; extension beyond observed limits admits the possibility that determining or counteracting causes differ elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater generality increases reliability (but still empirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: As empirical generalizations become more general (apply to a larger variety of things), they become more certain because they demonstrate resistance to many potential counteracting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law true of many diverse instances suggests few causes can affect it; however, even the greatest generalizations remain empirical and must be tested across constituent sub-kinds unless causation is demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require stronger proof to establish exceptions to more general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires much more evidence to establish an exception to a highly general empirical law than to a more special one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more general the law (e.g., 'all animals' vs 'all crows'), the less credible an alleged exception will appear, and correspondingly stronger proof would be necessary to overcome the accumulated evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground universal propositions about higher Kinds on examination of all sub-kinds (unless causation shown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal propositions respecting superior Kinds, when not derived from causation, should be founded on separate examination of every known sub-kind included in the larger Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer universality for a higher Kind from inspecting only a portion of its sub-kinds; where possible, examine each infimæ species or show causal connection that warrants generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations (Most A are B) are empirical and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of the form 'Most A are B' are not laws of causation or ultimate truths; they are empirical approximations whose certainty depends on the proportion of concordant to discordant instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such propositions as useful for practical guidance or as steps toward universal truths, but not as foundations for strong deductive reasoning without further refinement or causal understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations are valuable as materials toward universal truths
rubrics_metrics.description: In science, 'Most A are B' statements are useful chiefly as materials for, and steps toward, discovering universal truths; science's proper end is not to stop at majority-statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to circumscribe the majority by some common character (a cause or distinguishing property) to elevate an approximate generalization into a universal law useful for deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes for ascertaining approximate generalizations: direct and indirect
rubrics_metrics.description: One can establish 'Most A are B' either by direct observation of frequency (counting instances) or indirectly by examining the frequency of the causes or marks that produce B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to decide if most Scotchmen can read, one could (a) observe many Scotchmen (direct), or (b) check whether most Scotchmen have been sent to schools that teach reading (indirect). Often both modes are combined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer certain marks or causes for individual cases when available
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, replace uncertain approximate indications with certain criteria (recognizable causes or marks) when judging particular instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., rather than relying on 'most people speak truth', examine witness-specific marks (honesty, accuracy, interest) to judge the credibility of a particular testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply numerical averages only within observed limits and only to average cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical precision (e.g., 'nine out of ten A are B') gives a quantifiable probability of error, but only within the limits of time, place, and circumstance embraced in the observations and only for cases that are not known to be atypical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply genus-level averages to specific species or to instances known to be under particular circumstances; averages are most useful for large-number guidance (e.g., insurance tables) and less so for individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining approximate generalizations: addition vs deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When using multiple approximate generalizations together, they may combine either (a) by addition (independent propositions each applying to the case, increasing probability), or (b) by ratiocination/deduction (one proposition only applies via the other, which generally yields a lower net probability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of addition: two independent witnesses each saying the same fact increases probability. Example of deduction: one person's testimony that he heard another reduces to a single chain and is less reliable than two independent testimonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations often inadequate for scientific deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of their imprecision, most approximate generalizations are of little use for scientific deduction except as interim steps toward identifying causes or narrower, universal propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For scientific progress, seek to refine 'Most A are B' into propositions with causes or distinguishing marks so they can be employed in deduction and not merely in probabilistic practical judgement.
